newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russian banks respond warily to new gold rules.
newsitem.headline: Russian banks respond warily to new gold rules.

text.p: Russian banks say new rules erasing a Soviet-era ban on the holding of bullion have not enticed them to plough funds into the gold mining industry.

Commercial banks, eyeing the Central Bank of Russia's third day of quotes for the metal, said the scrapping of state prices was not enough to convince them it was safe to put big cash into the beleagured mining sector.

"They are saying the market has been liberalised, but nothing has been liberalised," said Dmitry Ignyatyev, head of precious metals at the Russian Banks' Association, adding banks wanted the right to quote their own prices and to export freely.
"They're going to scare us away from financing output, which is extremely risky without proper legislation and guarantees."

Russia has the world's third largest reserves and was its fifth largest gold producer in 1995, when it mined 142 tonnes. But that was sharply down on the 122-124 tonnes mined in 1996, and 1997 output is forecast to slip to 80-110 tonnes.

The cash-strapped goverment and the central bank hope the lessening of some restrictions on trading gold will encourage banks to advance money to mines. But the banks say this will not really happen until all Soviet-style restrictions on exports are scrapped and other risk factors diminish.

The central bank, which quotes gold at two percent above and below London fixes, depending on whether it is selling or buying, has said it wants a free and open gold market in Russia, where output has sagged around a quarter since peaking at around 160 tonnes a year in the mid-1980s.

"The central bank's new system doesn't entirely suit us," said Pavel Khoroshev, precious metals head at Rossiisky Kredit, a bank licensed to trade gold. "We need certain terms, like the right to export any time, so we can do swaps, loans etc."

Commercial banks are waiting to see how the central bank follows through with a promise to sign documents next week allowing them to export bullion. Until that happens, Russia's new banks may find financing mines unappealing.
"Financing gold output is risky and hard to control," Khoroshev said, adding most banks' investment portfolios were in oil, metals and timber. "Gold will have to wait a few years."

Industry sources estimated banks would hold 20 tonnes of gold by 1998. Banks had already contracted for 14 tonnes from 1997 output, stepping in where the cash-strapped state failed. The central bank will buy the rest, giving it control over most of Russia's supply.

One source quoted a senior Western bullion source as saying Russia's central bank wanted to be the Bank of England, South Africa's Reserve Bank and a clearing centre, all in one. "It wants to regulate prices, and advance cash for mining, and control exports, all at the same time," the source said.
Banks said recent changes allowing private citizens to acquire bullion legally for the first time since 1917 would not result in an exodus of gold out of Russia, since private citizens cannot export.
But with Russia's bullion prices nearly three times below per-gram prices for jewellery, inflation-conscious citizens might begin shifting savings from jewellery and dollars into bullion.
"There will be fewer people buying jewellery and burying it in the ground at the dacha," said a Rossiisky Kredit spokesman.
Private citizens can buy gold in two ways -- as jewellery at salons, where it carries a 20 percent value-added tax, or by opening up special accounts at banks, where it is stored.
Soon individuals will be able to buy bars at exchanges. But they will have to pay a three percent commission and the weights will range from 100 grams to one kg, more than most can afford.
"Those who are really rich will diversify their savings into gold," Khoroshev said. "But it's too early to say gold will edge out the dollar as Russians' preferred savings instrument."
